strategy:
1. Approach and rationale
Use parallel-tempering simulated annealing on the exact discrete objective. Each replica moves along randomly selected feasible chords of the capped simplex, sometimes taking a short symmetric step and sometimes sampling the whole chord. Accept downhill moves and accept uphill moves with a temperature-dependent Metropolis probability; periodically exchange states between neighboring temperatures. Keep the best exact-scoring state separately, so an exploratory uphill move can never erase the best solution found.

This is materially different from the supplied trust-region LP and the earlier epigraph/SLSQP, smoothed-gradient, pairwise line-minimization, and differential-evolution approaches. It uses no gradient, linearized lag model, nonlinear solver, pairwise coordinate minimizer, or population recombination. Its main purpose is to explore the full feasible set and cross barriers associated with changes in which lag is worst. Chord proposals preserve the mass constraint by construction, and all candidate decisions use the exact evaluator score.

The feasible set is a convex polytope, and a direction with zero coordinate sum stays in its mass hyperplane. On a fixed chord, both the full-chord hit-and-run proposal and the defined symmetric local proposal are reversible in exact arithmetic. Metropolis acceptance therefore has a well-defined temperature interpretation before numerical roundoff handling; replica exchanges use the corresponding product-distribution acceptance ratio. These are mathematical properties of the proposal and acceptance rules. Whether finite runs discover a better construction is a heuristic: the objective is nonconvex and nonsmooth, mixing can be poor, and neither this method nor the target score is guaranteed. Retain a validated supplied parent and the uniform vector as fallbacks, and make no global-optimality or untested-improvement claim.

2. Mathematical specification
For runtime integer n with 1 ≤ n ≤ 999, represent the samples by h in R^n. Set dx = 2/n and s = n/2. The feasible set requires 0 ≤ h_i ≤ 1 for every index i and sum_i h_i = s. If a valid-length `initial_h_values` is supplied, its length defines n; do not change resolution or interpolate it. Otherwise use a valid requested `n_points`, with default 47.

For every integer lag d from −(n−1) through n−1, define i0 = max(0,−d), j0 = max(0,d), m = n−|d|, and q_d(h) = sum over r=0,...,m−1 of h_(i0+r) times (1−h_(j0+r)). The set of these 2n−1 finite-support sums is exactly the set returned by the full linear correlation, possibly in reversed lag order. Thus the objective to minimize is C(h) = dx times max_d q_d(h), computed for candidate decisions by `max(np.correlate(h, 1.0-h, mode='full')) * dx`. Include every lag, including both directions and the shortened boundary overlaps. Do not use circular correlation or replace boundary sums with an identity involving the full mass.

For a feasible state x, choose a direction v with sum_i v_i = 0 and Euclidean norm one. The feasible chord consists of x+t v for t in [a,b]. For each coordinate with v_i > 0, its contribution to the interval is [−x_i/v_i, (1−x_i)/v_i]. For v_i < 0, it is [(1−x_i)/v_i, −x_i/v_i]. Intersect these intervals across coordinates; coordinates with v_i = 0 impose no restriction. In exact arithmetic a ≤ 0 ≤ b, and every point on the chord satisfies the mass and box constraints.

Use a mixture of two proposal kernels with fixed probabilities. With probability 0.20, choose t uniformly on [a,b] (full-chord hit-and-run). Otherwise choose t uniformly on [−rho*(b−a), rho*(b−a)] and reject the proposal as a self-transition if t is outside [a,b]. For a fixed direction and any line through the feasible set, the chord length and local radius are the same when moving in either direction; the direction distribution is sign-symmetric. These kernels are symmetric in exact arithmetic. The energy is the exact score C. At temperature T > 0, accept a proposed y with probability min(1, exp(−(C(y)−C(x))/T)).

For replica slots ordered from cold to hot, let their temperatures be T_i and T_j and their current energies E_i and E_j. The log acceptance ratio for swapping their states is (E_i−E_j)*(1/T_i−1/T_j). Accept the swap if this value is nonnegative, or otherwise with probability exp of that value. The global best is maintained independently of all chain states. No surrogate objective is used for acceptance or final ranking.

3. Implementation procedure
1. Write one complete program defining `run(seed=42, **kwargs)` at top level. Use float64 NumPy arrays and `math` as needed. Define every helper at module top level, with no nested functions, closures, or lambdas. Provide helpers for option parsing, capped-simplex projection, feasibility, exact scoring, roundoff repair for chord proposals, start generation, direction generation, chord bounds, proposal generation, Metropolis acceptance, and replica exchange. NumPy and math are sufficient; do not use filesystem or network I/O or an optimization solver. Read the provided `initial_h_values` defensively; never redefine, serialize, reconstruct, or hard-code its entries.

2. Resolve n and the parent inside `run`. In a guarded conversion, convert the supplied global to a float64 one-dimensional runtime array. If its flattened length is between 1 and 999, use that length as n, even if the entries later prove unsuitable. If no valid parent length can be read, parse `kwargs.get('n_points', 47)` as an integer-valued scalar in [1,999]; on failure or an out-of-range value use 47. Do not change a usable parent’s resolution.

A parent is usable as candidate data only if its entries are finite and lie in [−1e−8, 1+1e−8]. If it is already in [0,1] and its mass error is within 2e−14*max(1,n), preserve its values unchanged as a candidate. Otherwise restore the near-bounded finite parent with the capped-simplex projection. Reject parent values outside the stated near-bound tolerance or a failed projection, but retain n from the valid parent length. Store a separate feasible parent copy as a persistent fallback. Parse `seed` as an integer, use 42 on conversion failure, reduce it modulo 2^32, and create a local `np.random.default_rng`; do not use global random state.

3. Implement the capped-simplex projection P(z). Require shape (n,) and finite values; otherwise return failure. Clip finite input entries to [−1e12,1e12]. Find lambda such that sum_i clip(z_i−lambda,0,1) = s by bisection on [min(z)−1, max(z)+1]. At each midpoint, if the clipped sum exceeds s, raise the lower endpoint; otherwise lower the upper endpoint. Perform at most 100 iterations and stop if floating-point arithmetic cannot move the midpoint. Form h_i = clip(z_i−lambda,0,1) using the final midpoint. Correct the remaining residual s−sum(h) deterministically: for a positive residual, visit coordinates in increasing order and add at most 1−h_i; for a negative residual, subtract at most h_i. Make at most three passes and stop when the residual magnitude is at most 1e−13*max(1,n). Do not rescale. Return failure unless the result is finite, exactly within [0,1], and has mass error at most 5e−12*max(1,n). This is the joint box-and-mass projection used for parent repair, starts, restarts, and final repair.

4. Implement `is_feasible(h,n)` to require exact shape (n,), finite entries, exact bounds 0 ≤ h_i ≤ 1, and absolute mass error at most 5e−12*max(1,n). Implement `exact_score(h,n)` to return positive infinity if feasibility fails. Otherwise compute the literal full linear correlation `np.correlate(h, 1.0-h, mode='full')`, multiply its maximum by 2.0/n, and return a Python float. Catch correlation errors and reject nonfinite scores. If the correlation call raises, a slow fallback may enumerate d from −(n−1) to n−1 using q_d as defined in section 2; this is the same exact finite-support objective, not a circular or truncated surrogate. Never clip or alter h inside the scoring helper.

5. Implement a bounded start generator. Always propose uniform h_i=0.5. If a usable parent exists, also propose, algorithmically, the parent itself, its reversal, its complement, its complemented reversal, and parent plus seeded Gaussian noise at standard deviations 0.025, 0.08, and 0.20. In every case preserve a copy of the original feasible parent separately. Also propose a block vector with the first floor(n/2) entries equal to 1 and, for odd n, the next entry equal to 0.5; an alternating 0/1 vector; cosine patterns 0.5+0.45*cos(2*pi*q*i/n) for q=1 and q=2; a seeded uniform random vector; and a seeded beta(0.5,0.5) vector. Without usable parent data, use the same patterns and random vectors without parent-derived proposals. Generate all patterns by array operations and formulas, not explicit tables.

Project every proposed start. Discard failures and deduplicate candidates whose maximum absolute coordinate difference from a stored start is below 1e−10. Score every distinct feasible start exactly and update the persistent best only for a finite score at least 1e−12 lower than the saved best. Uniform and the projected parent, if available, remain separate fallbacks even if duplicated or excluded from the chain-start list. Store copies of every fallback and best vector.

6. Calibrate the temperature ladder in program. From a fixed copy of the current best, generate up to 24 pilot proposals using the same proposal procedure with rho=0.08 and full-chord probability 0.20. Score each exactly, record positive score increases relative to the fixed reference score, and still add any improvement to the persistent best. If there are positive increases, let d_med be their median and set T_hot = clip(d_med/(-log(0.8)), 1e−5, 0.02). If there are none or the calculation is invalid, use T_hot=0.002. Set T_cold=max(1e−6, 0.02*T_hot). For M replica slots, assign T_j = T_cold*(T_hot/T_cold)^(j/(M−1)) for j=0,...,M−1, so slot zero is coldest. If a pilot option is zero, use the stated fallback temperature. Keep the ladder fixed during a run except for the explicitly described state restarts.

7. Construct M chain states from the scored starts. Set the cold slot’s state to the persistent best. Fill other slots in order with distinct feasible starts where available, skipping duplicates of already assigned states. If fewer than M distinct states exist, try up to 30 projected Gaussian perturbations of the best or a start, cycling standard deviations 0.025, 0.08, and 0.20. If all attempts fail or duplicate, use a valid duplicate state. Compute and store an exact score for every slot. For n=1 the only feasible vector is uniform; skip all direction moves and return the best fallback.

8. Implement direction generation without a dense matrix. With probability 0.70, draw n independent standard normal values and subtract their mean to obtain a dense zero-sum direction. Otherwise choose uniformly among the distinct block lengths min(n,4), min(n,8), and min(n,16), with each length at least 2; choose a contiguous non-wrapping block start uniformly, draw independent standard normals on that block, and subtract their block mean, leaving other entries zero. For either type, remove residual sum roundoff by setting the last active component to the negative sum of the other active components, normalize to unit Euclidean length, then remove any residual sum roundoff once more on that component. If the norm is nonfinite or at most 1e−14, reject this direction. The distribution of direction type, block length, block start, and Gaussian values must not depend on the current state.

9. Implement chord bounds from the coordinate formulas in section 2, intersecting all nonzero direction coordinates. Reject nonfinite bounds or a chord width at most 1e−14. For replica j use fixed local fraction rho_j=0.02+0.12*j/(M−1). With probability 0.20 draw t uniformly over the whole chord. Otherwise draw t uniformly from [−rho_j*(b−a), rho_j*(b−a)] and return no proposal if t falls outside [a,b]. Form y=x+t*v only for a valid t.

Before scoring y, apply a numerical-only roundoff repair: reject nonfinite entries or any coordinate outside [−1e−12,1+1e−12]; clip only these tiny excursions to [0,1], distribute the resulting mass residual in increasing coordinate order over available capacity, and reject if the initial or remaining mass error exceeds 5e−11*max(1,n). Return the repaired vector only if `is_feasible` accepts it. Do not apply a general capped-simplex projection to ordinary chord proposals: in exact arithmetic the chord already enforces the constraints, and a general projection would change the proposal kernel. The roundoff repair is limited to floating-point error; final candidates are jointly projected before return.

10. For each sweep, update each replica once, in slot order. Generate a proposal from that slot’s current state and rho_j. Skip failed proposals and proposals whose maximum coordinate change is at most 1e−14. Compute `exact_score` for every remaining feasible proposal. For delta = new_score−current_score, accept unconditionally if delta ≤ 0. If delta > 0, accept only when a fresh uniform random value is less than exp(−delta/T_j); if delta/T_j exceeds 745, reject without evaluating the exponential. On acceptance, replace that slot’s state and score. Whenever any feasible scored candidate is more than 1e−12 below the persistent best, store a copy as the new best. The best is never replaced by an uphill move.

11. After all replica proposals in a sweep, attempt adjacent swaps on alternating parity: for even-numbered sweeps try pairs (0,1), (2,3), and so on; for odd-numbered sweeps try (1,2), (3,4), and so on. For each pair use the log ratio in section 2 and accept with probability min(1,exp(log_ratio)); for a negative log ratio compare log of a fresh uniform variate with the ratio to avoid underflow. Swap both state vectors and scores. The temperatures remain attached to slots.

Track sweeps since the last persistent-best improvement. When a sweep improves the global best, reset the counter; otherwise increment it. Set patience=max(50, floor(steps/5)). If patience is reached and restart budget remains, reinitialize slots j from max(1,floor(M/2)) through M−1, leaving colder slots intact. For each reinitialized slot, choose the best vector or a start in alternating order, add seeded Gaussian noise using standard deviations 0.03, 0.08, and 0.18 cyclically, project with the capped-simplex helper, and score exactly. If projection fails, use the selected feasible base. Update the persistent best if warranted, increment the restart count, and reset stagnation. If patience is reached after the restart budget is exhausted, terminate early. Restarts do not add sweeps to the configured limit.

12. Catch failures at the smallest practical scope: a bad direction or proposal skips that move; an invalid score skips that candidate; a failed restart leaves the existing slot and saved best intact. An exception affecting the search loop must not discard the parent, uniform, or best fallback. All loops have explicit bounds. After search, consider the persistent best, feasible parent fallback if available, and uniform. Recheck and recompute exact scores, then select the lowest-scoring feasible candidate. Jointly project the selected vector once more and use the repaired version only if it is feasible and its recomputed exact score is no higher than the saved selected score. Otherwise retain the saved feasible vector. If any final check fails, use uniform and recompute its exact score.

4. Search choices and useful variations
Use these defaults without preliminary experiments: parent length when valid, otherwise n_points=47; for n≤64 use M=5 replicas, 800 sweeps, and at most 2 restarts; for 65≤n≤128 use M=4, 400 sweeps, and at most 1 restart; for 129≤n≤256 use M=3, 120 sweeps, and at most 1 restart. For n>256, still validate and exact-score the bounded baseline starts and fallbacks but skip replica evolution to bound work on one CPU. Skip all search for n=1. These limits do not alter the chosen grid resolution.

Parse optional `chains`, `steps`, `restarts`, and `pilot_moves` in guarded top-level helpers. Ignore malformed values and use the size-based defaults. Clamp chains to 2..8, steps to 0..2000 for n≤64, 0..800 for 65≤n≤128, and 0..200 for 129≤n≤256; clamp restarts to 0..3, 0..2, and 0..1 respectively; clamp pilot_moves to 0..64. For n>256 force steps to zero. A zero steps or restart setting disables only that search stage, not input validation, projection, exact scoring, or fallback selection. Use 24 pilot moves by default and the specified fallback temperature when no positive pilot increase exists.

The defaults for full-chord probability 0.20, dense-direction probability 0.70, local fractions, and temperature ratio 0.02 define a complete search. Meaningful bounded variations a coder may choose are 3–6 chains for n≤64, more or fewer sweeps within the stated caps, full-chord probability 0.10–0.35, dense-direction probability 0.5–0.85, local fractions about 0.01–0.20, or a cold-to-hot ratio about 0.005–0.10. The defaults require no preliminary tuning. Any added adaptation must be a bounded in-program rule; do not claim it reaches the target. The exact lag set, objective, mass, bounds, parent-resolution rule, exact-score selection, and fallbacks are correctness requirements, not choices.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use
Use float64 throughout and run all replicas sequentially on the available single CPU. Each state and proposal uses O(n) memory; the starts and replicas together use O((M+S)n), where S is a small bounded start count. A correlation result has 2n−1 entries. Do not construct a dense lag-by-coordinate matrix, Hessian, all-pairs tensor, or circular FFT surrogate. Exact score evaluation through `np.correlate` has work proportional to the direct finite-support correlation, approximately O(n^2); the size-dependent limits bound the number of evaluations, and search is skipped above n=256. The parent grid n=47 remains unchanged.

Reject nonfinite inputs, directions, chord bounds, proposals, and scores. Use the joint capped-simplex threshold projection for starts and final repair, not separate clipping and rescaling. Use the small roundoff-only correction for chord proposals and reject corrections larger than its stated tolerance. Metropolis exponents are nonpositive when evaluated; underflow to zero is a valid rejection, and large positive acceptance log ratios accept directly. Failed trials do not modify chain states or the persistent best. The explicit sweep, pilot, chain, restart, and patience limits provide termination. Parallel tempering and finite starts remain heuristics for this nonconvex problem, not a certificate of optimality.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract
The generated program must define `run(seed=42, **kwargs)` at top level and return exactly `(h_values, c5_bound, n_points)`. It must read the supplied parent defensively, use a valid parent length as n, and never redefine or hard-code `initial_h_values`. Before scoring or storing any candidate, check shape, finite values, bounds, and mass. Use the exact full linear-correlation expression inside the program for every candidate eligible to update the best and for the returned score; use the all-lag direct sum only as an equivalent scoring fallback if the correlation call itself fails.

Maintain a feasible projected parent fallback whenever parent data can be repaired and a uniform fallback at all times. Preserve the original parent values unchanged when they already satisfy the constraints. Accept an uphill proposal only by the specified Metropolis rule, but replace the persistent best only after a feasible candidate has a finite exact score more than 1e−12 lower. Recompute the selected score after final repair. If parsing, projection, scoring, restart, or search operations fail, return the lowest-scoring surviving feasible fallback, with uniform as the final guaranteed vector. The returned h must be one-dimensional of length n, finite, within [0,1], and have sum n/2 within the projection tolerance; return its recomputed exact score as a Python float and n as an integer. The coder supplies source operations only; execution and score measurement happen later.
